JSON: Name: ai_tools_is_success_utas Title: PLS-SEM and randomized intervention evaluation of how system, information, and service quality of generative AI tools affect student use benefit, satisfaction, and perceived net benefits in higher education Short Hypothesis: Enhancing the information_quality and service_quality of generative AI tools causes increases in student_use_benefit and student_satisfaction, which mediate an increase in perceived_net_benefits. Related Work: Prior work operationalizes digital system success with the DeLone–McLean IS Success Model and analyzes adoption outcomes through the Stimulus–Organism–Response framing. Empirical studies using PLS-SEM and variance-based SEM routinely find information quality and service/support quality to be strong predictors of satisfaction and perceived benefit in e-learning contexts; system/technical quality often shows weaker or mixed direct effects on satisfaction or learning gains. Existing work is dominated by cross-sectional surveys, small to moderate convenience samples, single-institution case studies, and self-reported outcomes; objective usage logs and experimental manipulations are rare. Limitations across current approaches include reliance on common-method self-report, limited causal identification, sparse mediation testing with large samples, lack of multi-institution datasets in underrepresented regions, and insufficient ablation of individual quality dimensions versus combined effects. Abstract: This research pipeline tests whether improvements in information and service quality of generative AI tools causally increase student-perceived use benefit and user satisfaction, and whether those organism-level responses mediate gains in perceived net benefits in higher education. The approach combines a multi-institution cross-sectional PLS-SEM analysis (latent constructs from validated scales plus objective usage logs) with a cluster-randomized semester-long intervention that manipulates information quality, service quality, and system quality across course sections. The main contribution is a unified empirical strategy that integrates predictive SEM, mediation testing, and randomized controlled contrasts to move beyond correlation and establish causal pathways from specific quality dimensions to academic outcomes. Expected outcomes are quantified path estimates, mediation effects, and cross-validated predictive metrics that identify which quality levers produce the largest effect on student satisfaction, use benefit, and perceived net benefits in a higher-education setting. Experiments: 1) Observational PLS-SEM dataset: collect N >= 600 students from 3–5 higher-education institutions (Oman/GCC), each record containing: validated Likert-item scales for system_quality, information_quality, service_quality, use_benefit, user_satisfaction, net_benefits; LMS logs and AI-tool API metrics (session count, prompt count, tokens, latency); academic outcomes (assignment scores, course grades, time-on-task). Preprocess: confirmatory factor analysis, compute AVE, CR, Cronbach alpha. Primary analysis: PLS-SEM with bootstrapping (5,000 resamples) to estimate path coefficients, indirect effects (mediation), R2, f2, Q2_predict, SRMR. Baselines: (A) DeLone–McLean baseline model (IQ, SQ, SER -> Satisfaction/Use -> Net Benefits); (B) Linear regression and OLS; (C) propensity-score matched SEM using observed covariates. Ablation: sequentially remove SQ, IQ, SER from model and compare ΔR2, ΔQ2_predict, AIC/BIC. 2) Cluster-randomized controlled trial (semester, cluster = course section): target sample >= 400 students distributed across four arms (control, information_quality_enhancement, service_quality_enhancement, system_quality_enhancement), minimum 100 students/arm. Interventions: (a) IQ arm: curated AI prompt templates, domain-tuned content filters, contextualized examples; (b) SER arm: dedicated live/async support, in-product guided help, tutorial micro-modules; (c) SQ arm: performance optimizations, lower-latency instances, UX adjustments. Pre/post measurements: same validated scales plus objective logs and course outcomes. Analysis: ANCOVA on post-treatment latent scores controlling baseline, SEM mediation of treatment -> UBT/UST -> NBT, between-arm contrasts (Cohen's d), multi-group invariance tests. Secondary analyses: per-protocol and intent-to-treat, sensitivity to attrition, VIF for multicollinearity, Harman's single-factor test for common-method bias. Evaluation metrics: path coefficients (β) and 95% CI, p-values (bootstrap), R2 and adjusted R2, Q2_predict, SRMR, RMSE, MAE, effect sizes (Cohen's d), change in objective academic outcomes (Δgrade, Δtime-on-task) with p-values. Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Sampling and generalizability: multi-institution sample may still be regionally constrained (GCC/Oman) and not representative of global higher-education contexts. 2) Self-report and common-method bias: primary constructs measured by surveys are susceptible to social desirability, recall bias, and inflating correlations. 3) Confounding and contamination: observational SEM cannot fully rule out unobserved confounders; RCT arms risk contamination when students share resources across sections. 4) Intervention operationalization: decomposing and isolating information_quality vs service_quality treatments may be difficult in practice because design changes overlap. 5) Attrition and noncompliance: semester-long RCTs risk dropout or varying adherence affecting internal validity. 6) Measurement error: latent scales could have limited temporal stability; objective usage logs may be noisy or incomplete. 7) Small effect sizes: true causal effects may be modest and require larger samples than planned for adequate power. 8) Multicollinearity: high intercorrelation among quality dimensions could inflate standard errors and obscure individual effects. 9) Privacy and ethics: collection of LMS logs and AI API data entails data-protection concerns and potential nonresponse. 10) Resource and operational limits: rolling out tailored interventions across many course sections requires coordination and compute resources which may constrain sample sizes and fidelity.
